prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping of atoms, that opened a new regime of precision in time and frequency measurement.

statement.case_for: B010 is the strongest candidate to carry into the final ballot. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the trade-off between atom number and motional shifts, and Ye's group turned it into clocks at about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, with the many-body and coherence physics that came with it. The result is not a single claim: it has been reproduced and compared across many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL), which is exactly the independent confirmation I ask for first. As an instrument builder I know how much calibration and systematics work sits behind a number like that, and here the work is understood in detail. The consequences are concrete: relativistic geodesy over millimetre height differences, bounds on drifting constants and a pending redefinition of the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the list, two people who each made a decisive and distinct contribution, and seven of eight members placed it on their ballot, four in the top three. In my opening ballot I put IceCube first because it is my own field and a new observational window, but I should not let field affinity decide a prize when the committee evidence points elsewhere.
statement.case_against: The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so part of the headline impact is still prospective, and the committee already honoured precision-timekeeping neighbours: the frequency comb in 2005 and ion-clock work (Wineland) in 2012. A critic can say lattice clocks are a refinement of an established metrology programme rather than a new window on nature, and that the instrument improvement is larger than the discovery content. There is also an adjacency question with the 2005 prize, and contributors outside the credited names (Lemonde, Takamoto, ion-clock groups) will be argued for. If the committee values a first observation of a new phenomenon over a better measurement, IceCube or twisted bilayer graphene carries more discovery content.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first: a discovery found in nature that opened a window on the universe and answered the cosmic-ray origin question, with the 2013 flux confirmed since by TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane.
responses.response: I agree on the science and I ranked B061 first myself. The scientific case is strong and the detection is secure. My difficulty is practical. Only three of us ranked it, one placing it fifth, and the attribution among Halzen, Karle and Spiering is less clean than you suggest, because the collaboration is large and source identification is still thin. You rightly want expert reports to weigh the founding group, and I cannot say that issue is resolved. I would keep B061 as my first alternative and see whether the committee can build support for it, but I cannot call it the consensus choice today.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected TEM first as a tool that opens a door to phenomena that could not be seen before, with a compact three-person attribution, and ranks IceCube fifth as arguably early for source identification.
responses.response: I share your respect for instruments that break a long-held limit. I ranked B039 fourth, and the Scherzer barrier argument is a good one. My reservation is that it was backed by only three of us and by a wide gap in placement, from your first place to Eriksson's seventh, and that Eriksson himself notes the discovery content is weaker than the instrumentation content. On IceCube I partly agree: the diffuse flux is firm and I would not call the detection early, but I accept that identifying the sources is incomplete. By that same maturity standard the lattice clock is on firmer ground, since many laboratories reproduce 1e-18 performance.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first for the theory-to-experiment link and a clean platform, and places the lattice clock sixth, noting that its redefinition of the second is pending and that instrument prizes carry less discovery content.
responses.response: I take the redefinition point seriously and list it as an uncertainty. I would answer that the science does not depend on the redefinition: the 1e-18 comparisons and the tests of relativity already stand on their own. On B051 we differ in emphasis rather than fact. It is outside my expertise, so I defer to you and Mehlig, but Johansson and Mehlig both flag that the superconducting mechanism is unresolved and that Cao and Fatemi sit outside the credited names, and I want to know whether the committee regards the discovery as secure enough while the interpretation is still moving. That is why I keep it as an alternative and not as my preference.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a new measurement capability that extended time and frequency metrology by orders of magnitude, with a clean two-person credit, and notes that Lemonde, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups sit outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree, and your point about the other contributors is the one I would take into the final discussion. Takamoto's 2005 demonstration and the SYRTE work are real, and the citation should be worded around the lattice-clock concept and its realisation so that it stays accurate. I do not think they displace Katori and Ye, since the proposal and the accuracy record are distinct, decisive contributions. Where I would push you is on the 2025 circuit prize and B041: you rank circuit QED second, and I value its demonstrations, but I regard B041 as the less urgent candidate because of that adjacency.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first because a clean idea was made quantitative through accurate atomic-structure theory, reproduced in many laboratories, and notes the approaching redefinition of the second.
responses.response: Your argument on atomic-structure theory (magic wavelengths, blackbody shifts) is persuasive and is the part I cannot judge from the instrument side. It strengthens the attribution case, because the clock works only through understood systematics. I would still ask you how much weight you give the 2005 and 2012 prizes: if the committee treats those as already covering the field, the lattice clock needs to be argued as a distinct achievement, and the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice, not time and frequency in general.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes as leaving room for a distinct lattice-clock prize.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should weigh on timing or whether the existing 1e-18 results already suffice.
Whether B061 can attract support beyond Danielsson, Olsson and me, and whether the credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering can be defended against the large collaboration.
How far the unresolved superconducting mechanism and the omission of Cao and Fatemi should count against B051, which I am not qualified to judge.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B010, B051 or B041. For B061 I work in astroparticle physics at KTH and am not an IceCube member as far as my profile shows, but I belong to the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, and my field is close enough that colleagues may wish to weigh my view on B061 with that in mind. I also flag a wider connection on B012 (WMAP) and B057 (ATLAS/CMS) only as shared detector expertise, not as a personal tie.
